analysis.one_liner: Bans the poisons Compound 1080 and federal use of M-44 cyanide predator devices.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban Compound 1080 and M-44 poison devices never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned the manufacture, possession, and sale of sodium fluoroacetate (Compound 1080), a poison used to kill predators, and required the government to collect and destroy existing stocks, paying people who turned theirs in. It would also have barred any federal agency from using M-44 devices, which spring sodium cyanide into the mouths of coyotes and other predators. The bill never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who live near or recreate on rangeland would be protected from accidental poisoning: Compound 1080 and M-44 devices are not selective and have killed dogs, family pets, and non-target wildlife, and poisoned carcasses can endanger people and other animals. Humans have also been killed by M-44s. The bill would also benefit wildlife and the people who value it, and would compensate private holders who surrender stocks of Compound 1080 for destruction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents, pets, wildlife, and ranch hands

how_it_helps.text: Bans manufacture, processing, possession, and sale of Compound 1080 outright, with criminal penalties of up to 2 years in prison for possession after an 18-month phase-in.
Requires the Agriculture Secretary to inventory, collect, and destroy all remaining stocks of Compound 1080, and to compensate non-federal holders who turn theirs in.
Prohibits any federal entity from using M-44 devices, which propel sodium cyanide and have killed people, pets, and non-target animals.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and private users of predator poisons would lose these tools, and the compensation and destruction program would be funded out of the USDA's Wildlife Services Program budget. Livestock producers who rely on poison devices to control coyotes and other predators would bear the cost of switching to other methods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Livestock producers and Wildlife Services users

drawbacks.text: Ranchers and wildlife managers would lose two lethal tools for controlling coyotes and other predators that kill livestock, and the bill does not fund replacement methods.
Compensation for surrendered stocks comes out of the Wildlife Services Program's own budget, which could shrink that program's other activities to pay for the buyback.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety and wildlife benefits of removing two highly toxic, indiscriminate poisons from use are real and permanent, while the cost is borne narrowly by livestock producers who would have to use other predator-control methods, and modestly by taxpayers through the buyback funded within Wildlife Services. The main honest objection is effectiveness: banning these devices does not stop predation, it only changes the method.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and their subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: DeFazio introduced the bill on December 18, 2007 with 10 original cosponsors, near the end of the first session of the 110th Congress.
It was referred to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, and Judiciary — a fragmented referral that requires three separate committees to act before a bill can move.
It was then split among three subcommittees: Environment and Hazardous Materials, Crime Terrorism and Homeland Security, and Horticulture and Organic Agriculture.
No committee or subcommittee held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it out, and the House never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Users of Compound 1080 and M-44 devices — chiefly the livestock industry and USDA's Wildlife Services program — kept their poison tools because the bill never advanced. No one in the general public gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Livestock producers and federal predator-control agencies

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban Compound 1080 and prohibit federal M-44 use.

for.name: 35 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in subcommittees for over a year until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; it never reached a floor vote, so no formal party split was recorded.

industries.note: The federal agency that deploys M-44 cyanide devices on rangeland would have been barred from using them, and its budget would have funded the Compound 1080 buyback. Its interest in keeping these tools ran against the public's interest in not being poisoned.

Ranchers would lose poison devices used to kill coyotes and other predators that attack livestock, forcing a switch to other methods. Some ranchers also work and recreate on the same land where these poisons endanger their families, dogs, and working animals.
The bill banned manufacture, processing, and sale of sodium fluoroacetate outright, eliminating the market for the product.
